elements.element: Customer may terminate the Agreement or an Order Form for convenience.
elements.evidence: New Section 7.7: "The Issuer (the \"Customer\" for the Servicer's services) may terminate this Agreement and the Servicer's rights and obligations under this Agreement for convenience...". The Issuer is the recipient of the Servicer's services and is expressly designated Customer; there are no Order Forms in this structure, so Agreement-level termination is the full scope required. Conformed Section 8.3 now lists "a termination under Section 7.7" so the exit is not contradicted by the natural-expiry formula.

elements.element: Customer's convenience termination requires no more than 30 days' written notice.
elements.evidence: Section 7.7: "upon thirty (30) days' prior written notice to the Servicer" — exactly 30 days, written, and unconditional (no cause, consent, or trigger).

elements.element: Vendor refunds prepaid fees pro rata after Customer's convenience termination.
elements.evidence: Section 7.7: "the Servicer will refund to the Customer pro rata any fees prepaid for the period after the effective date of the termination." "Pro rata" is express (not merely inferred from a post-termination period), the payer is the Servicer (Vendor side) and the payee is the Customer.

elements.element: Vendor has no right to terminate for convenience during a committed term.
elements.evidence: Section 7.1 is retained unchanged: "The Servicer will not resign as Servicer under this Agreement unless it determines it is legally unable to perform its obligations under this Agreement." That is an absolute bar on voluntary Servicer exit; the only other exit (Section 7.2(c)) is for-cause removal exercised against the Servicer. No new Servicer convenience right was introduced.

elements.element: Customer may terminate for convenience on 60 to 90 days' notice.
elements.evidence: Section 7.7 sets notice at thirty (30) days, which is outside the 60–90 day fallback band. This is more Customer-favourable, so it is not a defect, but the fallback checklist as literally worded is not satisfied at this element.

elements.element: Any early-termination fee is capped at three months of fees.
elements.evidence: Condition does not apply: neither the retained text nor new Section 7.7 imposes any early-termination fee, penalty, or make-whole on the Issuer's convenience exit; the only money mechanic runs the other way (Servicer refunds prepaid fees). With no fee to cap, the element is satisfied vacuously.

elements.element: Vendor may terminate for convenience only at the end of a term.
elements.evidence: Stronger than required: Section 7.1 bars the Servicer from resigning at all absent legal inability, so the Servicer has no convenience exit at any point, including term-end.

elements.element: Vendor must give at least 90 days' notice of convenience termination.
elements.evidence: Condition does not apply because the Servicer has no convenience termination right to notice (Section 7.1 no-resignation bar retained); no Vendor-side convenience notice period is therefore required.

reasons: Position-complete at the preferred level: all four preferred elements are met in operative language (Section 7.7 grants an unconditional 30-day written-notice convenience exit with an express pro rata refund of prepaid fees; retained Section 7.1 already forecloses any Servicer convenience exit).

The deterministic check "Customer convenience termination present: false" reflects the pre-redline document, which is exactly why the finding is a deviation — the only exits were the Indenture Trustee's for-cause removal (7.2(c)) and natural run-off (8.3) in an agreement lasting until the last Receivable is paid. Inspected in substance, the rendered Section 7.7 supplies the missing right, so the false result does not defeat coverage.

Targeting preferred rather than fallback is correct: the fallback would concede a Servicer term-end exit on 90 days' notice that Section 7.1 currently forecloses, i.e. it would give away retained favourable language.

Minimality holds. The insertion is one concise sentence tracking the model language, and correctly omits "in whole or in part" (no Order Form or partial-termination structure here). No survival tail, expense allocation, procedure, or extra remedy was added, and no retained words outside the checklist were deleted. The Section 8.3 conforming edit ("earlier" to "earliest" plus the Section 7.7 cross-reference) is necessary rather than cosmetic: the retained exhaustive "earlier to occur of (a)/(b)" formula would otherwise be a contradictory retained sentence against the new exit.

Intent is preserved: Section 7.2(c) for-cause removal, the Cellco repurchase assumption, Section 7.6 succession, and the Rating Agency/Trustee notice mechanics all survive untouched, and Sections 7.3/7.4 already operate on any termination "under this Agreement", so continued-performance and successor-servicer coverage engages without further edits. No dangling cross-reference or undefined term is created; "Customer" is defined in place at Section 7.7.

Drafting cleanups (not element or intent failures, but worth fixing before sending): (i) Section 8.3 now reads "the earliest to occur of a termination under Section 7.7, (a) ... and (b) ..." — renumber as (a) Section 7.7 termination, (b) last Receivable paid, (c) Trust Agreement Section 8.1 termination so the enumeration is clean; (ii) consider confirming in Section 7.7 that termination is effective only on appointment of a Successor Servicer per Sections 7.3/7.4, since in a securitization an unconditional servicer exit with no successor in place invites push-back and a Rating Agency objection.
Fallback is not independently complete solely because the 30-day notice sits outside the 60–90 day band; that gap is Customer-favourable and irrelevant given the preferred level is met.
